title: Creating your first wiki
description: Create a hosting account and a wiki instance.

sections.heading: Your hosting account
sections.html: Register at the hosting portal. Follow any email verification or account approval steps shown there. If approval is required, wait for the decision before creating an instance.

sections.heading: Create the wiki
sections.html: Choose New Instance in the dashboard and complete the form. The portal shows the address, initial administrator credentials, service expiry, and resource limits. Save the credentials and open the wiki to begin. Wiki accounts and hosting accounts are separate. What your wiki includes lists everything it can do.

title: What your wiki includes
description: Everything a new wiki can do, and what is switched on from the start.

sections.heading: Pages and editing
sections.html:
Pages are written in Markdown, with a live preview beside the editor. You can import a .md or .txt file into a page, attach files and images, embed videos, and export any page as Markdown or PDF or print it. Drafts are saved while you type, so closing the tab does not lose your work.

Pages live in categories, which can be nested, and the sidebar search finds pages and categories by name. Administrators can import or export many pages at once as Markdown files. The visual page builder lays out a page without writing Markdown; on this service it has to be allowed for your instance first.

sections.heading: History and review
sections.html:
Every save is kept. A page’s history shows what changed between two revisions and lets you restore an earlier one.

With Page Governance an editor can reserve a page while working on it, or protect it so that only they can edit it, and changes proposed by people without edit rights wait for approval. Another administrator can lift a protection after a 72-hour wait. Deletion Slowdown holds a deleted page for 48 hours so an administrator can bring it back.

sections.heading: People and access
sections.html:
Every account has a role: user, editor, administrator or owner. Administrators can also build custom roles from individual permissions, and limit reading and editing to particular categories. New members join with an invite code or by signing up, and sign-ups can require approval.

A wiki is private by default. Public read access is optional and, on this service, has to be allowed for your instance. Temporary Accounts removes accounts, pages or elevated roles on a date you choose.

sections.heading: Working together
sections.html:
• Kanban boards with tickets, comments, attachments and a history of changes.
  • Canvas diagrams that mix text, images and video with links to wiki pages.
  • Chats and Groups for direct messages and group conversations inside the wiki.
  • Announcements for banners shown across the site.
  • User Profiles with a bio, an avatar and a map of each person’s contributions.

sections.heading: Reading and learning
sections.html:
• Text-to-Speech reads pages aloud in English and Italian with Piper voices that run on the server rather than a third-party service, once the voices are installed there.
  • Assessments add polls and quizzes to a page, with points and limits on attempts.
  • Badges are awarded by hand or automatically, for example after a number of contributions.
  • Difficulty Tags label pages by level.

sections.heading: Administration
sections.html:
The interface is available in English and Italian, and administrators can add another language. EasyWiki mode, chosen when you create the instance, switches off the advanced features for groups that only need pages. Members can start a guided tour from their settings, and administrators can show it to everyone who joins.

The API Service gives scripts access through tokens limited to chosen areas. Custom Pages publishes content at an address you pick. Every member can download their own data from their Settings page, and Site Migration exports the whole wiki as one archive.

sections.heading: Switched on from the start
sections.html: A new wiki starts with Attachments, Audit, Canvas, Chats and Groups, Drafts, Kanban Board, Page History, Text-to-Speech and User Data Export enabled. If the first administrator picks the Easy setup, Attachments and Chats and Groups start switched off. The rest are one click away; see Managing plugins.

title: Inviting users and managing roles
description: Control who can read and edit your wiki.

sections.heading: Accounts and invitations
sections.html: Inside the wiki, use the administration pages to manage registration, invitations, and users. Give people only the role and permissions they need. A hosting collaborator and a wiki editor have different responsibilities and permissions.

sections.heading: Page access
sections.html: Check category and page permissions before sharing content. Test the result using an ordinary user account. Removing a user’s editing permission does not automatically make previously public content private.

title: Configuring wiki settings and privacy
description: Set the wiki name, appearance, and access policy.

sections.heading: Site settings
sections.html: Wiki administrators can change the site name, appearance, language, enabled features, and registration settings. Hosting limits and domain permissions are managed separately by platform administrators.

sections.heading: Private content
sections.html: Choose the intended visibility for pages and categories, and review links before sharing them. Administrators of the hosted service can access server data for operation and support; consult the privacy policy.

title: Creating and editing pages
description: Write pages, organize categories, and add files.

sections.heading: Pages and history
sections.html: Create a page in a category you can edit. Use the editor to write content, preview it, and save. The history view lets you review previous versions and restore an earlier version when your permissions allow it.

sections.heading: Uploads
sections.html: Use the editor’s upload controls for images and attachments. The wiki shows the allowed formats and size limits. The hosting service also limits total storage. Keep original files outside the wiki when you need an independent copy.

title: Managing plugins
description: Turn the optional parts of your wiki on and off.

sections.heading: Where to find them
sections.html: Open Settings from the top bar and choose Plugins under Admin Operations. Disabling a plugin hides its pages and menus and keeps its content, but it also switches the plugin’s own settings off, for example direct messages, group chats and chat attachments for Chats and Groups. Enabling it again does not turn those back on, so check the plugin’s settings afterwards. Disabling Text-to-Speech also deletes the audio it generated.

sections.heading: The built-in plugins
sections.html:
These ship with every wiki. The ones marked on are enabled when a wiki is created.

  • Announcements: banners shown across the site.
  • API Service: a REST API with personal tokens, each limited to chosen areas, and an audit log.
  • Assessments: polls and quizzes on a page, with points and attempt limits.
  • Attachments (on): files attached to pages.
  • Audit (on): a record of role changes, custom user tags and contributions.
  • Badges: awards given by hand or automatically.
  • Canvas (on): diagrams with text, images, video and links to pages.
  • Chats and Groups (on): direct messages and group conversations.
  • Custom Pages: content published at an address you choose.
  • Deletion Slowdown: deleted pages are held for 48 hours before they go.
  • Difficulty Tags: labels for the level of a page.
  • Drafts (on): drafts saved while you edit.
  • Kanban Board (on): boards, tickets, comments and attachments.
  • Page Governance: reservations, protection and approval of proposed changes.
  • Page History (on): revisions, differences and restoring an earlier version.
  • Temporary Accounts & Pages: accounts, pages and roles that expire on a schedule.
  • Text-to-Speech (on): pages read aloud by voices running on the server.
  • User Data Export (on): each member can download their own data.
  • User Profiles: profile pages with a bio, an avatar and a contribution map.

sections.heading: Plugins from elsewhere
sections.html: The Plugins page can also import a .bwplugin file written by someone else. A plugin is Python code and runs with the wiki’s own access to its data and network, so install only code you trust. On this service each wiki runs in its own container, and the operator can switch off every custom plugin on a wiki at once if one causes trouble.

title: Exports and backups
description: Keep copies of your content and understand restoration.

sections.heading: Export your wiki
sections.html: Open Settings, then Migration under Admin Operations, and in the Export Site section choose Download Site Export for a complete archive of the wiki: content, accounts, files and settings. It is the copy to keep, and the one to use if you move the wiki to your own server. For pages only, Markdown Import / Export exports them as Markdown files, and any single page can be exported as Markdown or PDF from its own menu. Members can download their personal data from their Settings page.

sections.heading: Platform backups
sections.html: Platform backups are managed by the service operator. Contact support to check which restore points and retention periods are available for your instance. Keep your own exports; a service backup is not a substitute for a copy you control.

title: Moving your wiki to your own server
description: Take a complete copy of your wiki and run it yourself.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.html: BananaWiki is free software under the GNU AGPL, and the source this service runs is published at {source_url}. A wiki moves across with its pages, accounts, history and files. You need an administrator account on the wiki you are moving, and somewhere to run the new one: a Linux server, or for a small group the desktop launcher, built from the source, on Windows, Linux or a Mac with Apple silicon.

sections.heading: 1. Export the wiki
sections.html:
In the wiki you are moving, open Settings, then Migration under Admin Operations, and in the Export Site section choose Download Site Export. The ZIP holds every table (accounts, pages, categories, settings, chats, boards and more), uploaded images and attachments, custom icons and the site configuration.

Keep the file private: it contains everything in the wiki, including account records.

sections.heading: 2. Install BananaWiki
sections.html:
Pick the route that fits:

  • A Linux server. From a checkout of the source, sudo ./banana install --mode wiki installs the service, and the deployment guide covers HTTPS, backups and updates.
  • Linux or macOS with Python 3.12 or newer. Follow the quick start in the README.
  • A desktop computer. The launcher is built from the source; see the desktop launcher guide.

Open the new wiki and finish the setup page with a temporary administrator account.

sections.heading: 3. Import the export
sections.html:
Signed in as that administrator, open Settings, then Migration, and under Import Site select the export file. Choose Delete all previous data and restore from file and start the import.

The temporary administrator is replaced by the accounts from the export, so sign in again with your usual username and password. Everyone else keeps theirs, except members who only ever signed in through the hosting portal: they have no password of their own, so an administrator sets one for them on the new server.

sections.heading: After the move
sections.html:
• Point your own address at the new server. Members sign in again, because sessions from the old one do not carry over.
  • Settings stored encrypted with the old server’s key, such as a remote text-to-speech token, read as empty and need to be entered again.
  • Automatic updates are off until you turn them on, and backups are yours to set up; the deployment guide explains both.
  • If anything did not come across, the original export is still your complete copy.

title: Managing accounts and instances
description: Review account access and operate your instances.

sections.heading: Account security
sections.html: Use the Account page to update your profile and password, manage two-step verification, and review active sessions. Save recovery codes privately. End sessions you no longer recognize.

sections.heading: Instance actions
sections.html: Pause stops an instance and keeps its files, and Resume starts the same wiki again. Terminating takes the wiki offline and keeps its data for the retention period shown in the portal; deleting it permanently, or the end of that period, removes the data for good.

title: Protecting your wiki
description: Use strong account controls and trusted extensions.

sections.heading: Accounts and content
sections.html: Use a unique password and enable two-step verification for your hosting account. Review collaborators and wiki roles periodically. Check visibility before publishing private material and keep independent exports of important content.

sections.heading: Report a problem
sections.html: Report suspected account compromise or service abuse to {contact_email}. For a vulnerability in the software, follow the private reporting instructions in its security policy. Do not post credentials or private wiki content in public issues.

title: Common issues and fixes
description: Find the next step when a wiki is unavailable.

sections.heading: A wiki does not open
sections.html: Check the instance status and expiry in the hosting dashboard. A paused instance may need to be resumed; if the account is suspended or declined, sort that out with the platform administrators first. Use the address the service assigned while diagnosing a custom-domain problem.

sections.heading: Ask for help
sections.html: Include the wiki address, approximate time, action attempted, and visible error. Describe whether the problem affects every user or one account. Never send passwords, backup keys, or authenticator codes.

title: Email verification
description: Add and verify a contact address when requested.

sections.heading: Verification steps
sections.html: If the portal asks for email verification, use the link sent to your contact address. Check spam folders and the address entered in Account settings. The portal shows when another verification email can be requested.

sections.heading: An address is no longer available
sections.html: Update the address from Account settings using your current password. If you cannot sign in, contact support for account recovery. Verification does not itself approve a pending account.

title: Instance expiry and renewal
description: Understand hosting time limits and recovery windows.

sections.heading: Service expiry
sections.html: The dashboard shows each instance’s service expiry. Ask support about an extension before that date if you want to keep using the hosted instance. These hosting limits are separate from the AGPL software license, which permits personal and commercial self-hosting.

sections.heading: Recovery
sections.html: After termination, retained data may be restored during the configured grace period. Contact support promptly and quote the instance address. Recovery cannot be promised after the retained files have been deleted. Export important content before expiry.

title: Using a custom domain
description: Connect a domain you control to an approved instance.

sections.heading: Permission and DNS
sections.html: A platform administrator must permit custom domains for your instance. Then open the domain controls, add the hostname, and copy the exact TXT verification record and serving record shown in the portal to your DNS provider. Keep those records in place.

sections.heading: Verification and HTTPS
sections.html: Request verification after DNS changes are visible. A hostname that is not verified within an hour expires: add it again and replace the TXT value with the new one the portal shows. HTTPS becomes available after verification and certificate issuance. If permission is revoked, verification expires, or the instance is suspended, the custom domain stops routing. The technical DNS guide explains the checks.

title: Using the hosting API
description: Create a token so a script can read your wikis and pause or resume them.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.html: The hosting API lets a script or another program read your account and your wikis, and pause or resume a wiki, without signing in to the portal. The operator of this service has to switch it on first. If your Account page has no API tokens section, the API is not available to your account.

sections.heading: Creating a token
sections.html: Open Account and go to API tokens. Give the token a name that reminds you where it is used, tick the scopes it needs, choose when it expires and confirm with your current password. The token is shown once, straight after you create it, so copy it then. If you lose it, revoke it and create another.

sections.heading: What a token can do
sections.html:
• account:read reads your username and contact email.
  • instances:read lists your wikis, and the wikis shared with you, with their status and storage.
  • instances:manage pauses and resumes a wiki.
  • admin:read, offered only to platform administrators, reads the approval queue and instance totals.

On a wiki someone shared with you, a token can do only what your collaborator permissions allow. The API cannot delete, reset or download a wiki; the portal still does those.

sections.heading: Using and protecting it
sections.html: Send the token in the Authorization header of each request, as Bearer followed by the token, to /api/v1 on this portal. For example, /api/v1/instances lists your wikis. Keep a token as private as a password and revoke the ones you no longer use. Changing or resetting your password revokes all of them. Switching the API off does not: your tokens stop working while it is off and work again when it is back on, so revoke the ones you no longer want. The API reference lists every request.

title: Contact and support
description: Contact the hosted service or contribute to the software.

sections.heading: Hosted service
sections.html: Email {contact_email} for account recovery, hosting extensions, domain permissions, or abuse reports. Include your portal username and wiki address when relevant, without passwords or keys.

sections.heading: Source and contributions
sections.html: The source is maintained at BananaSuite/BananaWiki under AGPL version 3. Use public issues for reproducible software bugs and feature requests, with private data removed. Read the contribution guide before opening a pull request.
